why.core: Your **digital footprint** is everything online that's about you, posted by you or by other people. It lasts, it spreads, and it's read by people you never pictured: future bosses, coaches, teachers, strangers. Knowing your **audience** helps you choose what to share and how to say it, so your footprint shows the real you at your best.
why.extend: A digital footprint is a public text you write over years, often without noticing, and partly written by others. Because digital texts persist, spread and get read out of context, managing your footprint means thinking deliberately about audience, purpose and the identity your language creates.

articles.title: Your digital footprint

body.support:
Your **digital footprint** is everything online about you. Some you made: posts, comments, gaming profiles. Some **other people** made: tags, photos, **screenshots**.

**It lasts.** Deleting a post doesn't delete screenshots.

**Lots of people see it.** Friends, family, teachers, and one day, a boss.

**The age rules.** Since **December 2025**, under 16s can't have accounts on apps like TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat. You won't get in trouble. The apps will. But gaming and messaging apps are still allowed. So your footprint still grows.

**Think about your audience.** You'd tell your mates news one way, and a boss another way.

**Build a good footprint.**

1. Search your name.
2. Delete things you don't like.
3. Check your **privacy settings**.
4. Ask before you post other people.
5. Write a good **profile**.
body.core:
Your **digital footprint** is everything online that's about you. Some of it you made: posts, comments, a gaming profile, a video. Some of it **other people** made: a team photo on a club website, a tag, a **screenshot** of something you sent.

**It lasts, and it spreads.** Deleting a post doesn't delete the screenshots. Group chats get forwarded. Things you posted at 13 can still be found at 18.

**More people read it than you think.** Your **audience** isn't just your friends. It can include family, teachers, coaches, and one day, employers deciding whether to give you a job.

**The age rules.** Since **10 December 2025**, people under **16** can't have accounts on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, YouTube, X, Reddit and Twitch. The platforms have to stop them, and they can be fined if they don't. Young people and parents don't get in trouble. But messaging and gaming apps, like WhatsApp, Discord and Roblox, aren't covered. So even if you're under 16, your footprint is still growing.

**Write for your audience.** You'd share the same news differently with your mates, your nan, and a boss. Online, your audience can be all three at once. That's why it pays to think about who might read something before you post it.

**Build a footprint you're proud of.**

1. **Search yourself.** See what comes up.
2. **Fix what you can.** Delete old posts you're not proud of, and ask friends to remove photos of you.
3. **Check your privacy settings,** so only people you choose can see your **private** stuff.
4. **Ask before you post** someone else.
5. **Write a strong profile.** A short, positive description of you, with real examples, can be the first thing a boss sees.
body.extend:
Your **digital footprint** is everything about you online. It includes what you create (posts, comments, profiles, videos). It also includes what others create about you (tags, photos, club and school websites, **screenshots**).

**Digital texts last and travel.** Deleting doesn't remove copies. Private messages can be forwarded. Old posts can come back years later, out of context.

**Your audience is wider than you think.** A post written for friends may be read by family, teachers, coaches and future employers, all at once.

**The age rules.** Since **10 December 2025**, platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, YouTube, X, Reddit and Twitch must take reasonable steps to stop under-16s holding accounts, or face large fines. There are no penalties for young people or their parents. Messaging and gaming services, such as WhatsApp, Discord and Roblox, aren't covered, so younger teens still build a footprint.

**Language creates identity.** Your word choices signal who you are and your relationship with your audience. The same news, written for mates, a grandparent or an employer, creates three different versions of you.

**Manage it on purpose.** Search yourself. Remove content you regret, or ask others to remove it. Review your privacy settings. Ask before posting other people. And write a strong public **profile** that shows your strengths, with evidence.

caseStudies.title: Would they hire you?

body.support:
A university in Queensland asked **396 Australian bosses** about social media. That was in **2019**.

What they found:

- **82%** said a person's social media affected what they thought of them.
- The worst thing you could do was **hurt** people online.

So what you post can affect getting a job.

But it can **help** too. Posts that show you're kind or hard-working are a plus.
body.core:
Researchers at the **University of the Sunshine Coast** asked a question. Does social media affect who gets a job?

They asked **396 Australian employers** from lots of different jobs. The study came out in **2019**.

Here's what they found:

- **82%** of employers said what a person posts online **affected** what they thought of them.
- The **worst** thing, they said, was using social media to **hurt** other people on purpose.

So what you post, and how you treat people online, can affect whether you get a job.

But it works both ways. A footprint can also **help** you. Posts that show you're kind, hard-working or good at something give a boss a reason to say yes.
body.extend:
A team at the **University of the Sunshine Coast** surveyed **396 Australian employers**. They asked how job seekers' social media affects hiring. The study came out in **2019**.

- **82%** of employers said a job seeker's social media **influenced** them.
- The worst behaviour, they said, was using social media to **harm** others on purpose.

So employers read your posts as evidence of character. They look closely at how you treat people.

The effect can be good too. Posts that show you're reliable, skilled and respectful can support your application.

source.name: Sutherland, Freberg & Driver — “Australian employer perceptions of unprofessional social media behaviour and its impact on graduate employability” (2019)

teacher.overview: Students learn what a digital footprint is (content they create, and content others create about them), why digital texts persist and reach unexpected audiences, and how the social media minimum age (from 10 December 2025) does and doesn't affect them. The literacy focus is audience: selecting language for different readers and relationships, and how language creates identity. They audit their own footprint privately and write a short public profile for a real purpose. The case study is a 2019 University of the Sunshine Coast survey of 396 Australian employers.
prep: Decide how students will search their footprint: at home, or on school devices with your supervision. Never require them to share results.
Have a few real (anonymous or made-up) profiles from job or club sites to show.
Check your school's policy on discussing social media accounts, especially for students under 16.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** others tag, photograph or screenshot you; club and school websites; gaming and messaging. From 10 December 2025, under-16s can't hold accounts on platforms like TikTok and Instagram; the platforms face penalties, not young people or parents. Steps: search yourself, fix what you can, check privacy settings, ask before posting others, write a strong profile.

**Sort:** premiership medal — OK; rant about your boss — rethink; uniform and street sign — rethink; congrats comment — OK; screenshot of a friend's message — rethink; put-down joke — rethink.

**Profile:** 1 who I am (no address); 2 real examples; 3 strength with proof; 4 interests; 5 purpose; 6 safe contact.

**Three audiences (samples):** grandparent — *Hi Nan, I got a weekend job at Crust Bakery! I start Saturday.*; job site — *Weekend shop assistant at Crust Bakery: serving customers, handling cash and closing up.*

**Case study:** 82% of employers were influenced by candidates' social media; using it to deliberately harm others was rated most unprofessional; it's evidence of how you'd treat customers and workmates; e.g. a video of your cooking, a club award, volunteering.

realityCheck: **Footprint searches are private.** Some students will find things that upset or embarrass them, including things others posted. Never ask them to share, and be ready to help with removal requests.
**The age rules are new.** Some under-16s still have accounts, or use family accounts. Keep the focus on skills, not on who's breaking rules. Young people don't get in trouble under the law.
**Platform lists change.** Check eSafety's list of age-restricted platforms before you teach.
**Image-based abuse is serious.** If a student discloses intimate images being shared, follow your school's child safety procedures; eSafety can help remove them.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It links straight to Build Your Resume and Nail the Interview.
